drivers.name: Price increase (5.1%)
drivers.evidence: 2026-09-28: 5.1% price increase → 195 units (x0.94 vs baseline); consistent with 5-15% demand drop for price hikes

drivers.name: Store closure (Mon)
drivers.evidence: Store closed Mon; typical weekly sales ~20% of total; no prior closure data, but closure effects are consistent with ~20% loss

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 207.6. The target week has no events but a price increase to $4.56 (+5.1%) and a store closure on Monday. Price increases reduce demand; a 5.1% increase with no prior promotion history suggests a moderate lift-down. The past 5% price increase (2026-09-28) led to a 44% drop (195 vs 207.6), so a similar effect is plausible. The store closure (Mon) removes ~20% of the week’s sales, but the baseline already includes 5% of sales from Monday. A 20% sales loss is consistent with past closures. The uplift model suggests no effect, but judgment overrides this due to the price increase and closure. Evidence is moderate, so shrink toward 1.0.

brief:
PRODUCT: Whole Milk 1 gal | category Dairy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-25 (2 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.56 (+5.1% vs regular price 4.34)
  planner notes: Store closed Monday for renovation

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 207.6 | 5%-95%: 133.7 - 290.1 | 10%-90%: 156.4 - 280.9

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-22% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
